Frieze

ArithmeticSequencesInvariants
Game: Fill a strip of numbered dots so that every little diamond follows the same rule; there is no winner and no loser.
How to play: Click the right half of a dot to add one, or the left half to take one away. Press Compute to fill the rest and Undo to step back.
Rows Colours
Look for the math

The original cut-the-knot page still embeds this Java applet. Its arithmetic frieze pattern grows from a few chosen numbers: every four dots at the corners of a small diamond obey one rule.

One rule for every diamond

The dots sit on two staggered rows: an even row has one more dot than an odd row, so each interior dot has two neighbours above and two below. The applet writes the new value at the far corner of a diamond from the three values already there. In the adding mode it uses down = left + right - top + 1; in the multiplying mode it uses down = (left × right + 1) / top. Ticking Simple leaves the + 1 out. Clicking a rule button, even the one already selected, clears the lattice. The page's own wording invites you to start on the left, but the applet lets you change any dot; this port keeps that behaviour and computes outward from the fixed top and bottom rows.

Checking the two formulas

Writing the diamond corners as a, b, c, d, the page claims a + d = b + c + 1 for addition and ad = bc + 1 for multiplication, with the 1 dropped in the simpler case. The logic test checks every computed diamond for rows 5 through 14 and confirms both claims, including the staggered rows (where the neighbours are the upper and lower right-hand dots). Each pass stops at the first blank dot in a row, which is why a row with no starting number is left alone.

Fractions, zeros and colours

The multiplying formula rarely divides evenly. The applet drops the fractional part of the answer — it truncates toward zero, even for negative numbers — so ad = bc + 1 holds exactly only when the division comes out whole. A zero in the middle gives a zero child, which quickly kills a multiplicative pattern, just as the page warns. The colours use remainders modulo 2 to 10: the maximum is 10, and changing it never changes a number, only the colour used to show it.

Why it is called a frieze

A frieze pattern repeats along a line: its symmetries include a translation along that line. There are exactly seven frieze groups, the seven symmetry types listed on the original page. Conway linked the multiplicative number patterns to triangulations of polygons. This small lattice repeats only as far as its edges allow, so it shows the arithmetic idea rather than an infinite strip.

Try a few seeds with 10 colours, then switch to Circles to see the repeating stripes and diamonds.
